paras: The lynching of David Dunce took place in late January 1888, when a mob took Dunce from the jail at a place the papers printed as Bell Green, Alabama, and lynched him. Dunce was held for the killing of W. R. Wilson at Russellville, Alabama, a few weeks earlier. The news travelled as a one-sentence telegraph item that ran in papers across the country within a week.

According to the dispatches, Wilson had been killed at Russellville a few weeks before the lynching, and Dunce was in jail as his killer. The papers stated flatly that Dunce "murdered" Wilson, though none reports a trial, and none gives Dunce's race or any detail of the killing.

A special dispatch from St. Louis dated January 28 said Dunce "was taken from the jail at Bell Green last night by a mob and lynched." A separate dispatch datelined Russellville the same day said the mob took him "to-day," while a Chattanooga dispatch of January 30 put the lynching on Friday night. None of the reports describes the mob, its size, how it entered the jail, or how Dunce was killed, and no jailer or officer is mentioned.
No report of an inquest, arrests or any official response appears in the coverage, and no follow-up story was found.

The story reached the white press in two main forms: the St. Louis special, printed on January 29 by the Memphis Appeal, the Wichita Eagle and the Savannah Morning News, and the Russellville dispatch, printed by the Los Angeles Daily Herald and later the Butte Semi-Weekly Miner. The Memphis Appeal and the Savannah paper headed it "Lynching in Alabama," while the Wichita Eagle and the Chattanooga dispatch carried in the Maysville Evening Bulletin punned on the name with "A Dunce Lynched." The Butte paper used "Murderer Lynched," and every version called Dunce a murderer without qualification or comment on the mob.

In the following days the item was condensed into news summaries and weekly columns, including the Sacramento Daily Record-Union, the Yorkville Enquirer, the Concord People and Patriot, the Kanabec County Times, two Dakota weeklies and Chicago's Citizen. Condensing introduced errors: the name was printed "Runce," "Bruce" and "Duncie," the town appeared in at least seven spellings, and the Sacramento brief called Dunce "an Illinois murderer." Several of these columns placed the item beside reports of other jail lynchings that week, at Amite City, Louisiana, and Plymouth, North Carolina, whose victims they identified as "colored" or "negro," while giving no race for Dunce.

The date is uncertain: the St. Louis and Chattanooga dispatches and the Yorkville Enquirer place the lynching on Friday night, January 27, while the Russellville dispatch says "to-day" (January 28) and later summaries say Saturday night or "the 28th." The Saturday versions may reflect the dispatch date rather than the night of the lynching, since the earliest report, dated Saturday, already spoke of "last night."
